title: India Has Opened Its Stock Market to Every Foreigner. NRIs Are No Longer the Only Ones Who Can Buy In.
excerpt: A sweeping FEMA amendment notified on June 12 lets any individual living outside India invest in listed Indian companies — ending a decades-old framework that restricted the route to NRIs and OCIs alone.
body:
India has quietly done something it has never done before: it has opened the doors of its stock market to every individual on the planet who lives outside its borders.

On June 12, the Ministry of Finance notified the Foreign Exchange Management (Non-Debt Instruments) (Third Amendment) Rules, 2026 — a set of changes that replaces the long-standing framework limiting portfolio investments to Non-Resident Indians and Overseas Citizens of India. Going forward, any individual person resident outside India can purchase and sell equity instruments of listed Indian companies on recognised stock exchanges, on a repatriation basis.

The amendment rewrites Chapter V of the FEMA Non-Debt Instruments Rules. Its heading has been changed from "Investment by Non-Resident Indian or an Overseas Citizen of India" to the broader "Investment by an Individual Person Resident Outside India Including a Non-Resident Indian or an Overseas Citizen of India." The word "individual" now replaces "NRI or OCI" throughout Rule 9 and Rule 12.

## What This Means in Practice

Under the amended Rule 12, any person living outside India — whether an NRI in Houston, an OCI in London, or a Japanese citizen in Tokyo — can buy and sell shares of companies listed on the BSE and NSE through a designated branch of an authorised dealer bank.

The individual investment cap remains at less than 10 per cent of a company's paid-up equity on a fully diluted basis. The aggregate ceiling for all such non-resident individuals stays at 24 per cent unless sectoral regulations allow otherwise. If an investor breaches the 10 per cent threshold, the excess must be divested within five trading days — or the entire holding gets reclassified as foreign direct investment, locking the investor out of further portfolio purchases in that company.

Transfer rules have also been updated. Rule 13 now allows any individual resident outside India to transfer equity instruments by sale or gift to another person resident outside India, subject to government approval in sectors that require it.

## The Safeguard That Stayed

One restriction survived intact. Investments that would transfer ownership or control of a listed Indian company to citizens or entities of countries sharing a land border with India — China, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, Myanmar, Afghanistan, and Bhutan — still require prior government approval. This mirrors the broader FDI framework that New Delhi tightened in 2020, originally aimed at preventing opportunistic acquisitions during the pandemic.

## Why It Matters for NRIs

For decades, the NRI-OCI route under FEMA was a privileged channel — a recognition that the Indian diaspora had a special economic relationship with the country. That channel now widens to include any foreign individual, which means the competitive landscape for Indian equities shifts.

The upside: greater global participation should deepen liquidity, tighten spreads, and improve price discovery on Indian exchanges. More buyers, in principle, means more capital.

The concern, voiced quietly by some wealth advisors, is simpler: the regulatory advantage that NRIs held — the ability to access Indian equities through a streamlined route — is no longer unique. The playing field has been levelled.

The amendment also arrives at a moment when India is making a broader push to attract foreign capital. The Reserve Bank of India recently eased overseas borrowing rules for banks, offered concessional forex swaps, and allowed leverage on NRI deposits. The finance ministry has been pushing for India's inclusion in the Bloomberg Global Aggregate Bond Index, with investor feedback expected later this month. The FEMA amendment fits the pattern: India is making it easier for global money to flow in.

The notification, dated June 12 and numbered 1/11/2025-EM, is already in effect.
